cases.title: Mattala Airport: 800 Hectares of Forest Cleared in an Elephant Area
cases.place: Mattala, Hambantota District, Southern Province, Sri Lanka

lenders.name: Export-Import Bank of China (China Eximbank)
lenders.role: Government concessional loan of RMB 1,225,602,725, about US$209 million on the AidData page and about US$190 million by a Sri Lankan government estimate, for the Mattala Rajapaksa International Airport. Framework agreement 23 December 2009; loan agreement 5 March 2010 (AidData record 33369).

cases.conditions: China Eximbank lent to the Government of Sri Lanka, which passed the money on to Airport & Aviation Services (Sri Lanka) Ltd. AidData record 33369 gives 2 percent fixed interest, a 20-year maturity, a five-year grace period, a 0.5 percent management fee, a 0.5 percent commitment fee and a zero percent penalty rate, and records no collateral, escrow account or sovereign guarantee. The Auditor-General's performance audit of the airport gives the same 2 percent rate and five-year grace period but says repayment runs 15 years from 2015, and reports that the Treasury paid Rs. 1,989,815,019 in interest and fees during the grace period, 2010 to 2015. Responsibility for repaying the loan moved to the General Treasury in 2017 (AidData). The airport was built by Chinese contractors; China Harbour Engineering Company is named by AidData as the implementing company.

cases.community: The Auditor-General's performance audit says the land given for the airport "had basically been a forest" of about 2,000 hectares, of which 800 hectares were used for construction and 1,200 hectares for outlying facilities. The audit says that because of the airport "the natural habitats of the wild animals in the area had been cleared," that this resulted in "the loss of the environmental equilibrium," and that the access road from Mattala to Lunugamvehera "had bifurcated the natural habitat." Using figures from the Southern Zonal Office of the Department of Wildlife Conservation, the audit records human-elephant conflict after the airport was built: 10 people killed in 2012, 3 in 2013, 9 in 2014 and 4 up to July 2015; 11 people hurt in 2013, 9 in 2014 and 2 in 2015; 99 cases of property damage in 2013, 135 in 2014 and 66 up to July 2015; and 22, 21, 28 and 11 wild elephants dead in the same four periods. The Sunday Times reported in August 2010, while clearing was under way, that workers were "clearing and setting ablaze large tracts of land," that electric fencing ran on all sides rather than leaving animals a way out, "leading to a large number of animals getting trapped there," and that a corridor of 500 metres beside the Malala Ara had been cut to about 100 metres after pressure from officials. Echelon reported that about 2,000 acres of trees and shrubs were cleared and that the site was a designated elephant management area. The Auditor-General and the then minister both said the site had no human habitation and that no families were moved, and no record of households displaced was found.
cases.killed_note: The Auditor-General's audit, using Department of Wildlife Conservation figures, records 26 people killed in human-elephant conflict in the area between 2012 and July 2015, and 82 wild elephants dead in the same period, which it attributes to conflict "after the construction of the Mattala International Airport." These deaths were not caused by the project or its contractors directly and are not counted here. A December 2020 Daily Mirror opinion article says Hambantota district recorded 405 elephant deaths and 127 human deaths in 2019, and attributes habitat loss to the airport together with other development projects; that district figure is not counted either.
cases.outcome: The airport opened on 18 March 2013. The Auditor-General found construction cost US$243.7 million against a planned US$209 million, and income of Rs. 48 million in 2013 and Rs. 136 million in 2014 against running costs of Rs. 2,153 million and Rs. 2,865 million. The elephant reserve called for in the airport's environmental assessment was still not gazetted in 2014, four years after it was marked out, so the Wildlife Department could not act against encroachment (Sunday Times). Sri Lanka suspended external debt service in April 2022, which covered this loan (AidData). In April 2024 the Cabinet approved handing airport management to Shaurya Aeronautics of India and the Airports of Regions Management Company of Russia for 30 years (News First).

cases.confidence_note: The clearing of about 800 hectares of forest, the habitat split by the access road and the human-elephant conflict figures come from the Auditor-General's own performance audit of the airport, which links them to the airport's construction. Two of the Sunday Times allegations from 2010 were denied at the time: the Central Environmental Authority chairman, Charitha Herath, said no such things were taking place at Mattala and that his officers inspected the site; an Airport & Aviation Services project official said all terms and conditions were being followed, that the Forest Department marked the trees and the State Timber Corporation removed them, and that 120 metres had been marked out on one bank of the Malala Ara. Figures for elephants displaced differ: Wikipedia says about 200, while a 2020 Daily Mirror opinion article says over 450 lost habitat to the airport and other projects together. The Auditor-General and the then minister both said the site was uninhabited and that no families were moved; no household displacement is claimed here.
cases.ecosystem: Dry-zone forest and scrub in the Hambantota elephant range, beside the Malala Ara and on a migratory bird route

lvwhy.project: A China Eximbank concessional loan of about US$190 to 209 million paid for the airport.
lvwhy.land: About 800 hectares of state forest in a marked elephant management area were cleared for construction, and 1,200 hectares more taken for outlying facilities.
